title: The Undertow of Anderlecht
premise: Casper Underhill has spent thirty years in the Anderlecht house he inherited from his mother, tuning pianos and listening to radiators, keeping himself as unrecorded as the song she wrote for him and never played twice. When a late-night radio broadcast airs that song—performed by a dying pianist who claims it was given to him—Casper's careful invisibility collapses, forcing him to confront why his mother gave the music away, what she fled, and what he has been refusing to inherit. As the pianist's health fails, Casper traces the song's journey through letters, a half-burned notebook, and the memories of neighbors who knew more than they said. In the end, Casper plays the song aloud at the pianist's bedside—claiming both the melody and his own name—and finally becomes an owner of his life rather than its tenant.
about_author: Ansel Galloway is the pen name of a former piano restorer who spent a decade working in Brussels before turning to fiction. Their stories about quiet trades and inherited silences have appeared in several European literary journals.

chapters.title: The Radiator Speaks First
chapters.summary: POV: Casper. A winter morning in the Anderlecht house; Casper tunes a client's upright while narrating how each radiator in his own home holds a different year of his childhood. He establishes his creed of invisibility: tune, listen, leave no trace. Emotional beat: tender melancholy, the comfort of routine that is also a kind of hiding.

chapters.title: A Tenant of His Own Life
chapters.summary: POV: Casper. Casper pays 'rent' to a cousin who technically owns the house, a fiction both maintain so neither must discuss inheritance. At the market, neighbors greet him warmly but know nothing true about him. Emotional beat: the loneliness of curated anonymity; first hint that someone is watching him too closely.

chapters.title: Static, Then the Song
chapters.summary: POV: Casper. Insomniac at 2 a.m., Casper hears a radio broadcast from a hospital charity concert: a pianist named Elias Verhoeven plays an untitled piece—and it is the song his mother composed for him and never recorded. The announcer says Verhoeven calls it 'the gift.' Emotional beat: vertigo; the past breaking through the floorboards.

chapters.title: What Mothers Keep
chapters.summary: POV: Casper. Casper searches his mother's locked writing desk for the manuscript and finds the drawer empty except for a photograph of her with a young man at a conservatory, 1971. Flashback fragments: her hands on the keys, her refusal to ever play the song twice. Emotional beat: grief sharpening into suspicion.

chapters.title: The Man Who Plays Other People's Music
chapters.summary: POV: Elias. Elias Verhoeven, terminally ill, rehearses in the hospital chapel and reflects on the night in 1974 when a frightened young woman pressed a handwritten score into his hands outside a Brussels concert hall, begging him to keep it alive because she couldn't. Emotional beat: guilt and devotion; he has kept a promise made to a stranger for fifty years.

chapters.title: Letters to No Address
chapters.summary: POV: Casper. Among his mother's effects, Casper finds unsent letters addressed only to 'E.,' never mailed, describing the song as 'the thing I cannot give you and cannot destroy.' He realizes she meant them for the pianist. Emotional beat: the ache of a mother's unfinished sentence.

chapters.title: The Cousin Who Counts
chapters.summary: POV: Casper. Casper's cousin Dirk arrives demanding the house be sold now that their mother's estate is 'settled,' pressing Casper to sign papers. Casper stalls, sensing Dirk knows something about the desk's missing contents. Emotional beat: rising pressure; the family machinery of erasure grinding forward.

chapters.title: Half-Burned
chapters.summary: POV: Casper. In the coal cellar, inside a rusted biscuit tin, Casper finds a scorched notebook: his mother's composition sketches, the song among them, pages torn out—the same pages Elias must have received. Someone tried to burn it. Emotional beat: dread; the discovery that the silence was engineered, not natural.

chapters.title: The Neighbor Who Remembered Everything
chapters.summary: POV: alternating Casper and Mrs. Okonkwo. Elderly neighbor Odile recounts 1974: Casper's mother fleeing a conservatory scandal involving a professor who claimed her compositions as his own, and a young pianist who helped her disappear. Emotional beat: revelation reframing the mother not as fragile but as brave.

chapters.title: Finding Verhoeven
chapters.summary: POV: Casper. Casper writes to the radio station, then drives to the hospital in Ghent, rehearsing sentences he cannot finish. He watches through glass as nurses attend to a frail old man whose hands still move over phantom keys. Emotional beat: fear of being seen colliding with the need to speak.

chapters.title: Two Strangers, One Melody
chapters.summary: POV: Elias. Elias receives Casper's letter and recognizes the surname instantly—he has waited decades for this visit and dreaded it. He confesses to his nurse that the song was never his to perform publicly, yet broadcasting it was deliberate: a beacon. Emotional beat: hope braided with shame.

chapters.title: Dirk's Version
chapters.summary: POV: Casper. Dirk reveals the family secret: their grandfather burned the notebook to protect the family name after the professor threatened litigation; the 'rent' arrangement was designed to keep Casper dependent and quiet. Emotional beat: betrayal curdling into clarity—Casper's invisibility was inherited, built by others.

chapters.title: The Professor's Shadow
chapters.summary: POV: Casper. Researching the conservatory archive, Casper finds the professor's published works containing passages identical to his mother's earliest sketches. Her 'theft' was invented; her flight was survival. Emotional beat: fury and vindication, and the terrible cost of the price she paid.

chapters.title: What the Radiators Kept
chapters.summary: POV: Casper. Back home, Casper listens to the house fully for the first time—not escaping into its sounds but hearing them as testimony: his mother practicing at dawn, the night she packed, the silence after. Emotional beat: reconciliation with memory; the house becomes witness, not hiding place.

chapters.title: An Invitation, Refused Twice
chapters.summary: POV: Elias. Elias invites Casper to visit; Casper's first reply is a refusal, his second is silence. Elias, weakening, records a message for the radio: he will play the song one final time, publicly, and names its true composer on air. Emotional beat: ticking clock; courage passing between generations.

chapters.title: The Broadcast
chapters.summary: POV: Casper. Listening alone, Casper hears his mother's name spoken aloud on national radio for the first time in fifty years. Neighbors call, Dirk rages, and Casper understands there is no returning to invisibility. Emotional beat: exposure as liberation; the door closing behind him.

chapters.title: Signing Nothing
chapters.summary: POV: Casper. Casper refuses Dirk's papers, claims the house outright, and begins restoring his mother's piano, which he has kept covered for three decades. Emotional beat: quiet defiance; inheritance accepted at last, on his own terms.

chapters.title: The Road to Ghent
chapters.summary: POV: Casper. Carrying the restored notebook and the unsent letters, Casper drives through rain to the hospital, composing and discarding apologies all the way. He arrives at dusk. Emotional beat: trembling resolve; every mile a word he owes.

chapters.title: Out Loud
chapters.summary: POV: alternating Casper and Elias. At the bedside, Casper gives Elias the letters and asks to hear the song once more—but this time he sits at the hospital's wheeled upright and plays it himself, badly, completely, saying his mother's name and his own aloud. Emotional beat: climax; grief, love, and claim fused into sound.

chapters.title: Last Measures
chapters.summary: POV: Elias. Elias, days from death, tells Casper the truth he withheld: the woman asked him not to find her son until the son came looking himself. He kept even that promise. They record the song together, four hands, one take. Emotional beat: grace; a promise completed on both ends.

chapters.title: The Recording
chapters.summary: POV: Casper. After Elias's death, the recording is released with full attribution. Casper endures interviews, Dirk's resentment, and strangers' kindness, discovering that being known does not devour him. Emotional beat: aftermath; visibility survived, identity stitched together.

chapters.title: Owner
chapters.summary: POV: Casper. One year later, Casper teaches piano tuning to a young apprentice in the Anderlecht house, the song framed above the piano, the radiators still talking. He plays the piece each morning—not as memorial but as signature. Emotional beat: resolution; the tenant has become the owner, of house, history, and voice.
